questions.question: What does BIO tagging stand for in Named Entity Recognition (NER)?
questions.explanation: BIO tagging is a standard scheme where 'B-' marks the beginning of an entity, 'I-' marks the inside, and 'O' marks tokens that are not part of any entity.

questions.question: Why is a Conditional Random Field (CRF) often used as the final layer in an NER model?
options: To enforce consistent label sequences (e.g., preventing I-ORG after O).
To speed up training on long sentences.
To remove stop words from the input.
To convert tokens into dense embeddings.
questions.explanation: A CRF models the transitions between labels, ensuring that the predicted sequence is globally optimal and follows rules like 'an I-tag must follow a B-tag or another I-tag of the same type'.

questions.question: What is the benefit of using 'word shapes' (e.g., 'iPhone' -> 'xXxxxx') as features in classical NER?
options: It captures capitalization and alphanumeric patterns that are strong signals for proper nouns.
It makes the model faster by reducing the vocabulary size.
It helps the model understand the meaning of the word.
It is a required step for transformer models.
questions.explanation: Proper nouns (names, organizations, locations) often follow specific capitalization patterns. Word shapes allow the model to learn these patterns without needing to see every possible word in training.

questions.question: Why is entity-level F1 considered a more accurate metric for NER than token-level accuracy?
options: Because token-level accuracy overstates performance by counting 'O' tags, and entity-level F1 requires exact span matches.
Because entity-level F1 is easier to calculate.
Because token-level accuracy only works for binary labels.
Because entity-level F1 doesn't require ground truth labels.
questions.explanation: Most tokens in a sentence are 'O' (outside). High token-level accuracy can be achieved just by predicting 'O' everywhere. Entity-level F1 requires the model to correctly identify the entire span and type of an entity.
